summary: Adds the equivalent of the JOSE typ (type) header parameter to COSE. This brings the benefits of explicit typing, as described in RFC 8725, to COSE objects. Its value syntax is the same as the COSE content type header parameter.

plainLanguage.summary: A label on a package saying what kind of thing is inside prevents it being opened wrongly. This adds that label to COSE messages.

questions: what is the cose typ header parameter
what is explicit typing in cose
what is the cose typ label value
subtitle: A header parameter that lets a COSE object say what kind of object it is.

tldr.problem: JOSE has a typ header parameter for declaring the type of a whole object, but COSE had no equivalent, so explicit typing could not be used to tell COSE objects apart.
tldr.mechanism: This document adds a typ (type) header parameter to COSE, with label 16, using the same value syntax as the content type parameter: an unsigned integer or a string content type.
tldr.outcome: Applications can use it to tell different kinds of COSE objects apart, which helps prevent confusion between them.

today: RFC 9596 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2024. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why COSE Needs a Type
sections.content:
COSE defines header parameters that parallel many of those in JOSE, but it had no equivalent of the JOSE typ parameter, which declares the type of the entire data structure. RFC 8725 recommends it for explicit typing, using typ values to distinguish between different kinds of JSON Web Tokens.

This specification adds the equivalent to COSE. Its syntax is the same as the existing COSE content type header parameter, so it allows unsigned integers from the CoAP Content-Formats registry and string media type values.
sections.plainLanguage: One system already had a type label and the other did not. Now both do.

sections.title: The typ Header Parameter
sections.content:
The typ parameter declares the type of the complete COSE object, whereas the content type parameter declares the type of the payload. It is meant for applications where more than one kind of COSE object could appear. Use is OPTIONAL.

COSE libraries ignore the value other than passing it through to the application. Any processing is application-specific, for example checking that the value is a particular media type and rejecting the object if not. The parameter MUST NOT be present in unprotected headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is for the program using the message, not for the toolkit that handles it. It must go in the protected part, where it cannot be changed unnoticed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The case for explicit typing of COSE objects is the same as in Section 3.11 of RFC 8725: it can prevent confusion between different kinds of COSE objects.

Applications that use explicit typing should reject COSE objects whose type value differs from what they expect in that context. They should also reject objects with no type parameter when one is expected.
sections.plainLanguage: If you expected a birthday card and the label says something else, or there is no label, do not open it as a birthday card.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA has registered typ (type) in the COSE Header Parameters registry with label 16 and value type uint / tstr. The value registry is the CoAP Content-Formats or Media Types registry, and the description is the content type of the complete COSE object.
sections.plainLanguage: The label got its official number, 16, in the public list of COSE labels.
